GDC-RR-3913ef0116.title: A pre-post single-arm pilot trial of a digital multicomponent intervention for self-efficacy enhancement among online support groups of primary caregivers of children with neuro-muscular disorders: SEE-NMD protocol.
GDC-RR-3913ef0116.authors: Aziz NI, Khalid W, Khan S.
GDC-RR-3913ef0116.abstract:
Introduction

Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) and Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) are progressive genetic neuromuscular disorders that impose substantial caregiving demands on families. In Pakistan, where disease-modifying therapies remain largely inaccessible, care is predominantly supportive, frequently resulting in psychological distress and diminished caregiver confidence. An individual's belief in their capacity to execute required behaviours, self-efficacy, is a recognised determinant of caregiving quality, yet evidence on caregiver self-efficacy in SMA and DMD within low-resource settings remains sparse. This protocol describes the methods for an exploratory, single-arm, pre-post trial. The trial aims to generate preliminary evidence on changes in self-efficacy following a multicomponent, digitally delivered intervention and its implementation feasibility among primary caregivers of children with SMA and DMD in Pakistan.

Methods and analysis

A single-arm, pre-post study design will recruit primary caregivers of children with SMA and DMD enrolled in the Treat-NMD Registry of Pakistan, with 40 caregivers per condition (80 total) analyzed as separate disease-specific cohorts. An eight-week intervention will be delivered via online support groups, comprising educational video clips, expert-led live sessions, pictorial guides, and progressively tapering audio reminders. The primary outcome, self-efficacy, will be measured using a culturally adapted, content-validated Urdu version of the DMD Caregiver Self-Efficacy Scale (DMD-CSES), assessed at baseline (T0) and eight weeks post-intervention (T1). Pre- and post-intervention scores will be compared using a paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, depending on the data distribution, with analyses conducted in STATA Version 17.

Ethics and dissemination

Ethical approval has been granted by the Ethics Review Committee of Aga Khan University (2025-11875-37040). Verbal informed consent will be obtained from all participants, and confidentiality will be maintained throughout the trial. The findings will be disseminated via peer-reviewed publications, conference presentations, and shared with the Treat-NMD registry network.

Trial registration name and number

NCT07356063, Date of registration: 11/January/2026.

GDC-RR-0754a1641c.title: Mental Health Effects of Social Media Use Among Adolescents Across Educational Stages: A Meta-Analysis.
GDC-RR-0754a1641c.authors: Han C, Meng Y, Yang L.
GDC-RR-0754a1641c.abstract: BackgroundThe link between social media use and adolescent mental health is widely studied, but its variation across developmental stages remains insufficiently clarified. This meta-analysis aimed to compare the differential associations among primary, middle, and high school students.MethodsWe systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Embase, and CNKI up to 1 February 2026. Eligible studies reported correlation coefficients between social media use and mental health in school-aged youth. Analyses were performed using Stata 17.0 with random-effects model, subgroup stratification, heterogeneity testing, publication bias assessment, and leave-one-out sensitivity analysis.ResultsTwelve studies with 15 effect sizes were included. Social media use was significantly associated with worse mental health (r = 0.308, 95%CI: 0.239-0.374, p < 0.001) with high heterogeneity (I<sup>2</sup> = 93.85%). The association differed significantly by stage (Q = 9.72, p = 0.008): strongest in primary school students (r = 0.367), followed by high schoolers (r = 0.334), and weakest in middle schoolers (r = 0.201). No significant publication bias was detected; results were stable.ConclusionsThe association between social media use and mental health varies significantly across educational stages, with primary school students being the most vulnerable. Developmentally tailored prevention and intervention strategies are needed for school-aged youth.

claudeReview.reviewBasis: The abstract as published by Europe PMC on 9 November 2026, plus the Crossref record for DOI 10.1177/13591045261487468. The full text was NOT read: the journal page was not fetched. Every verdict below is therefore about what the abstract states and about the design it describes, not about the paper's internal detail.
claudeReview.proposedTitle: A new meta-analysis says the effect is much bigger. Here is how I decided not to use it.
claudeReview.proposedAngle: A paper landed this week that would help the argument I make for a living, and I am not going to use it. Walking a parent through why is more useful than the number itself, because it is the same test they can apply to the next frightening headline.
claudeReview.oneStory: A meta-analysis published on 6 November reports a correlation between social media use and worse mental health that is far larger than the best powered studies have found, and it would be very convenient for anybody selling a solution.
claudeReview.oneTension: The number is real and peer reviewed, and it still should not change what you believe, because twelve studies pooled with ninety four percent heterogeneity is not stronger evidence than a representative cohort of twenty five thousand.
claudeReview.oneBelief: We judge a finding by its design and its spread, not by whether it points the way we already lean. We publish the ones that are awkward for us, which means we also have to decline the ones that flatter us.
claudeReview.oneTakeaway: When a study says the effect is bigger than you were told, look for two things before you believe it: how many studies went in, and whether they agreed with each other.

claims.claim: The pooled correlation between social media use and worse adolescent mental health was r = 0.308, 95% CI 0.239 to 0.374, p < 0.001.
claims.basis: Stated verbatim in the published abstract. The DOI resolves through Crossref and the online publication date, 6 November 2026, agrees with the index. This verifies what the paper reports, not that the figure is a good estimate of the real world association.

claims.claim: The association varies by educational stage, and primary school students are the most vulnerable group.
claims.basis: The subgroup test is Q = 9.72, p = 0.008, but it is splitting twelve studies and fifteen effect sizes across three school stages. A subgroup analysis on that few studies is badly underpowered and highly sensitive to which study sits in which bin. 'Most vulnerable' is also a clinical claim about children, and the underlying studies are correlational, so the design cannot carry it.

claims.claim: r = 0.308 is a reasonable estimate of the association between adolescent social media use and mental health.
claims.basis: Two reasons for caution, both from the abstract itself. The heterogeneity is I squared = 93.85 percent, which means the twelve studies disagree with each other enormously and a single pooled number describes none of them well. And the search included CNKI alongside the English language databases, so the sample is likely weighted towards Chinese cohorts, which the abstract does not break down. The funder is the National Social Science Foundation of China. None of that makes the figure wrong, and all of it has to be said before it is repeated.

claims.claim: This finding is larger than the association reported by the best powered work in this field.
claims.basis: It is substantially larger than the pooled estimates we have already verified, which sit near beta = 0.061 across 46 studies and 79 effect sizes. But r and a standardised beta are not the same quantity, so the comparison is directional rather than a clean ratio. Do NOT write that it is five or six times bigger. Write that it is much larger and that the metrics differ.

claims.claim: Social media use has mental health effects on adolescents.
claims.basis: The paper's own title says 'Effects' while its methods pool correlation coefficients. The abstract body correctly says 'associated with' throughout. The title overclaims relative to the design, which is worth noting precisely because the title is what gets quoted.

verifiedStatistics: r = 0.308, 95% CI 0.239 to 0.374, p < 0.001, the pooled correlation
stage estimates as reported: primary r = 0.367, high school r = 0.334, middle school r = 0.201
notQuotable: any total number of participants: the abstract gives the number of studies and effect sizes but no pooled N, and the dossier could not extract one
'primary school children are most at risk', which the subgroup analysis cannot support
any multiple comparing this to earlier estimates, because r and beta are different metrics
any UK prevalence, since no UK breakdown is given and the search included CNKI
claudeReview.evidenceConfidence: LOW to MODERATE for the pooled figure as a description of these twelve studies. LOW as a guide to what is true of UK children. The design is sound for what it is, a random effects meta-analysis with publication bias assessment and leave one out sensitivity testing, and the reported stability is in its favour. The heterogeneity, the small number of studies and the absent country breakdown are what hold it down.
limitations: I squared = 93.85 percent. The included studies disagree so much that one pooled correlation is close to meaningless as a summary.
Twelve studies is a small base for any meta-analysis and far too small for a three way subgroup split.
Correlation coefficients only. Any study design that reported something else is excluded, which biases the pool towards cross sectional work.
No country breakdown in the abstract, with CNKI in the search, so the geographic mix is unknown and may be heavily Chinese.

Exposure is 'social media use' as each original study defined it, which is the exact undifferentiated measure the protocol says not to accept. Duration, content, time of day and interaction are all collapsed.
Mental health is likewise whatever each original study measured.
Full text not read, so the study table, the weighting and the actual countries have not been checked.
contradictoryEvidence: The Greater Manchester #BeeWell cohort, 25,629 teenagers, found no evidence that time on social media predicted later emotional difficulties. That is a single large representative longitudinal cohort against twelve pooled correlational studies, and on design it is the stronger evidence. It is already the basis of GDC-049.

The 46 study, 79 effect size meta-analysis pooling to roughly beta = 0.061, which Przybylski has described as smaller than the effect of wearing glasses. Four independent groups reached broadly the same small estimate. That is the body of work this new paper sits against.

Orben and Przybylski's specification curve analyses, which show how much an estimate in this field moves with analytic choices. With I squared at 93.85 percent, that critique applies to this pool with unusual force.
whatThisDoesNotProve: That social media causes mental health problems in children. Every input is a correlation.
That primary school aged children are the group most at risk.
That the association is large in the general population, or in the UK.
That the earlier small effect estimates were wrong. A twelve study pool with this heterogeneity does not overturn larger, better powered work.
Anything about which children are affected, which is the question that actually matters to a parent.
claudeReview.mediaMisrepresentation: No media coverage found at the time of review, which is expected three days after publication. If it is covered, the predictable error is the title's own word: reporting 'effects' and a correlation of 0.308 as though social media has been shown to damage children's mental health, with the 93.85 percent heterogeneity and the twelve study base left out. Worth watching.
gdcBeliefs: The Wrong Villain: the response should be proportional to the evidence, and that cuts both ways. A study that inflates the risk is as much a problem as one that dismisses it.
We check our own work harder than anybody else's, because the argument we make commercially benefits from exactly this finding.
'Screen time' is not one exposure. A pool that collapses duration, content and context cannot tell a parent what to do on a Tuesday night.

productImplications.digitalPathwayOS: Nothing changes. This is not outcome evidence for anything we build, and we hold none.
productImplications.schoolLesson: The stage difference, if it survives better evidence, would matter for which key stage gets the comparison and feed lessons first. It is nowhere near strong enough to move the scheme of work now.
productImplications.parentTool: No change to the stage check. It remains three questions and a starting point, with no outcome claim.
productImplications.digi: No change. DiGi should not cite a figure like this at all.

claudeReview.recommendedAudience: The evidence literate part of the LinkedIn following: school leaders, safeguarding leads and the researchers who already correct this field. The parent facing Substack is the wrong venue, because the usable content is a methods lesson rather than something to do tonight.
claudeReview.urgency: Low. Nothing expires. The value is the reasoning, not the news.
unresolvedQuestions: Which countries the twelve studies are from, and how much of the pooled estimate is Chinese cohort data. The abstract does not say and the full text was not read.
The pooled N. Not in the abstract.
Whether the three stage bins each contain enough studies to be worth reporting. Needs the study table.
Whether any of the twelve overlap in sample with each other, which the protocol specifically warns about for pooled work.

GDC-RR-04ce5786d0.title: Risks and Opportunities in Digital Media Interventions for Youth: A Scientometric Review
GDC-RR-04ce5786d0.authors: Andrews O, Brons ME, Chaplinska I, Nikken P, Ina HK, Mary S, Schuengel C.
GDC-RR-04ce5786d0.abstract: Youth must navigate both the opportunities and risks associated with digital media. Thisscientometric review examined 120 empirical studies on digital media interventions for youthand used the 4C framework (content, contact, conduct, and contract) to map their thematic focus.Scientometric mapping techniques were applied to explore keyword co-occurrence patterns andcollaboration networks. Most interventions addressed either risks or opportunities separately(58.3%), whereas 39.2% combined risks and opportunities within the same 4C dimension. Only2.5% integrated multiple 4C dimensions. Interventions predominantly focused on content andconduct, with limited attention to contact and contract, including topics like social interactions,privacy, digital rights, and commercialization. Collaboration patterns were fragmented, withresearchers working within thematic clusters rather than across them, despite drawing on ashared conceptual foundation. These findings suggest that current interventions cover only partof the 4C framework. Future research should encourage more integrated, cross-dimensionalinterventions and stronger collaboration among researchers.

GDC-RR-d49a029e70.title: Evaluating Human-Robot Interaction With a Socially Assistive Robot in Pediatric Health Care: Mixed Methods Pilot Study.
GDC-RR-d49a029e70.authors: Leoste J, Rakić S, Marmor K, Krinal K, Soostar LH, Vink KM, Käver A, Aasma K, Beatty K, Leoste LB.
GDC-RR-d49a029e70.abstract:
Background

Socially assistive robots are increasingly explored in health care, but evidence from routine pediatric outpatient settings remains limited.

Objective

This study examined how contextual support and human facilitation shaped visitor interaction with the Temi V3 robot and which sociotechnical conditions were associated with practical acceptance according to staff.

Methods

A mixed methods pilot combined structured behavioral observation across baseline, poster support, and staff facilitation conditions with 4 staff focus group interviews. The observation unit was a visitor passage through the lobby zone; the qualitative sample comprised 12 staff members with direct exposure to the robot. Quantitative indicators were analyzed descriptively, and staff interviews underwent deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis.

Results

In total, 675 visitor passages (children: n=398, 59% and adults: n=277, 41%) were recorded (baseline: n=257; poster support: n=160; and staff facilitation: n=258). Looking at the robot increased from 8 (3.1%) passages at baseline to 30 (18.8%) with poster support and 80 (31%) with staff facilitation. Screen or app use increased from 2 (0.8%) passages at baseline to 4 (2.5%) with poster support and 14 (5.4%) with staff facilitation. Observer notes indicated stronger visible responsiveness among children, although age category was not linked to individual behavior codes. Staff emphasized role clarity, child and family value, human mediation, functional reliability, multilingual content, and organizational ownership.

Conclusions

Observed visitor interaction was higher with poster support and staff facilitation than at baseline. These descriptive findings and staff perceptions informed a provisional 4-domain framework comprising role clarity, interaction affordance, social mediation, and organizational embedding. The framework identifies potential implementation priorities; visitors' own experiences and acceptance require direct assessment.

GDC-RR-4cdb28660e.title: Neonatal malaria management: a global survey of current practice.
GDC-RR-4cdb28660e.authors: Sultanli A, Remppis J, Honkpehedji YJ, Reif C, Esen M, Adegnika AA, Bélard S.
GDC-RR-4cdb28660e.abstract:
Background

Neonatal malaria remains underrecognised despite persistent high neonatal mortality in endemic regions. Evidence to guide diagnosis, classification, and treatment during the first 28 days of life is scarce, and neonatal-specific recommendations are largely absent. We conducted an international survey to describe current practices in neonatal malaria management and identify gaps in care.

Methods

We performed an anonymous online survey of healthcare professionals involved in neonatal malaria care between April 2024 and July 2025. The questionnaire, available in English, French, Portuguese, and Spanish, was distributed through professional networks and targeted invitations, assessing screening practices, diagnostic approaches, disease definitions, treatment strategies, dosing approaches, and perceived challenges. Data were analysed descriptively.

Results

A total of 173 respondents from malaria-endemic and non-endemic settings were included; most (91%) were based in sub-Saharan Africa. Most (61%) reported diagnosing neonatal malaria at least once yearly and 39% at least once a month. Most respondents (72%) did not distinguish between asymptomatic and symptomatic neonatal parasitaemia, and half (49%) did not differentiate between uncomplicated or severe malaria in neonates. The most used drugs were intravenous artesunate and artemether-lumefantrine for oral treatment. Among those using oral therapy, 71% reported using paediatric formulations, while 38% crushed tablets prior to administration. Crushed tablets were mostly mixed with water (90%), followed by expressed breast milk (23%) and infant formula (20%). In a case vignette of neonatal malaria, 87% of respondents recommended inpatient management with initial intravenous artesunate (92%) followed by oral artemisinin-based combination therapy (66%) with treatment duration ranging from 1 to 10 days and follow-up within 28 days (33%).

Conclusions

This survey demonstrates consensus in antimalarial drug selection alongside significant practice variation in disease classification and dosing, highlighting the need for evidence-based guidelines and improved access to age-appropriate formulations for neonatal malaria management.

GDC-RR-26d109b285.title: Sensory Literacies in Early Childhood Education: A Multimodal Interaction Analysis of Olfaction‐Enhanced Shared Reading
GDC-RR-26d109b285.authors: Radel James Gacumo, Ingrid Midteide Løkken, Natalia Ingebretsen Kucirkova
GDC-RR-26d109b285.abstract: ABSTRACT Reading in early childhood involves the coordination of multiple senses and modes of meaning‐making. While multimodal literacy research has examined visual, verbal and gestural interaction, the role of the sense of smell in shared reading remains largely unexplored. This study explores how young children engage bodily and emotionally during shared reading of olfaction‐enhanced digital books in early childhood education and care (ECEC) settings. Drawing on video observations of five Norwegian children aged 4–5, the analysis employs multimodal interaction analysis to examine how gesture, gaze, talk and smell intersect during literacy participation. The findings show how olfactory cues became integrated into embodied and collaborative forms of engagement. Children's interactions included moments of curiosity, affective synchrony and sustained attention around olfactory encounters, with smell emerging in some interactions as a semiotic pivot around which sensory perception, affect and interpretation became interconnected. The study suggests that attending to olfactory modes can extend understandings of multimodal literacy by making visible the intersections between digital reading and embodied sensory participation. These insights contribute to discussions of inclusive and holistic approaches to early literacy in ECEC.

GDC-RR-159233af83.title: Implementation of canva-based learning media to develop object-classification skills in children aged 5–6 years
GDC-RR-159233af83.authors: Meiman Sartika Zega, Khairatun Nisa, Novi Cynthia Yusnita
GDC-RR-159233af83.abstract: This study described the implementation of Canva-based learning media to develop object-classification skills among children aged 5–6 years at TK Elpatisia Medan. It used a descriptive qualitative approach involving the principal, the Group B teacher, and 15 children. Data were collected through observation, interviews, and documentation. Data credibility was supported by source and technique triangulation and member checking, while analysis involved data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings indicated that Canva media was implemented through planning, classroom implementation, and evaluation. Visual presentations containing colors, shapes, sizes, and object categories helped make learning more engaging and supported children in comparing and grouping objects. The observations described children as generally able to classify objects by color and type, while classification by shape and size was generally at the level of developing as expected; some children still needed prompts and teacher assistance. Supporting factors included school leadership support, teacher capability, children’s interest in visual materials, and the availability of laptops and a projector. Challenges included unstable internet access, limited devices, distractions, differences in children’s learning pace, and preparation time. The study concludes that Canva can serve as a useful visual learning medium when accompanied by teacher guidance and adequate preparation.

GDC-RR-d1f9996f06.title: When perpetrators are also victims: latent profiles of traditional and cyberbullying among adolescents who bully in 42 countries
GDC-RR-d1f9996f06.abstract: Background Adolescents who bully others are not a homogeneous group: some confine their behavior to face-to-face settings, whereas others also bully online or are themselves victimized. This study aimed to identify profiles of bullying perpetrators based on their patterns of traditional and cyberbullying perpetration and victimization, and to compare these profiles on individual well-being, health-related risk behaviors, and family, peer, and school characteristics. Methods Data from the 2017/2018 Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) study were used. Latent class analysis was used to identify profiles based on indicators of traditional and cyberbullying perpetration and victimization among adolescents who reported bullying others (n = 48,465; 42 countries). Differences between profiles were explored separately for boys and girls using the Bolck–Croon–Hagenaars approach that takes into account classification error. Sensitivity analyses tested the robustness of the solution to alternative specifications of the sample, weighting, measurement, age-group categories, and frequency of bullying. Results Three profiles emerged: a traditional-only profile, a cyber-involved profile characterized by cyberbullying perpetration, and a multiple bully-victim profile of adolescents who both bullied others and were bullied in traditional and cyber contexts. For both genders, the multiple bully-victim profile was the least favorable, with lower levels of perceived health and life satisfaction, increased occurrence of psychosomatic complaints, greater risk behaviors, lower family and peer support, less ease of communication with their mothers, and more negative school experiences. Problematic use of social media increased from the traditional-only to the cyber-involved profile and was greatest in the multiple bully-victim profile. On most other variables, the cyber-involved profile fell between the other two. Sensitivity analyses mostly supported the three-profile solution, although the cyber-involved profile was not recovered using a stricter criterion related to the frequency of bullying behavior. Conclusions The adolescents under study who engage in bullying behaviors do not constitute a homogeneous group; rather they show distinctive involvement patterns. Those who both bully and are bullied across settings fare poorly on several dimensions of their lives and thus interventions and prevention programs should be designed to deal with the different behavioral and psychosocial profiles.

GDC-RR-e923851b08.title: Decoding Digital Risk: Comparing Parent and Teen Reports of Teens' Online Activities.
GDC-RR-e923851b08.authors: Young E, Sharpe JD, Michael S, Welch P, McKinnon II
GDC-RR-e923851b08.abstract: As youth engage with digital media and technologies, parents face evolving challenges in balancing their benefits and risks. Despite recommendations to support parents in promoting teens' healthy digital habits, research suggests that parents' perceptions of teens' online activities often differ from teens' own reports. Using data from 522 parent-teen pairs, this study examined discrepancies in parent versus teen reports of parental digital mediation practices and parental knowledge of teens' online activities. Weighted prevalence estimates and measures of parent-teen discordance were calculated, accounting for the complex survey design. Findings revealed consistent discrepancies, with parents generally overestimating their knowledge of teens' online activities; however, discordance was lowest when parents engaged in digital monitoring strategies. These findings may inform approaches that help parents develop a more accurate understanding of teens' online activities and risk exposure while supporting teens' digital safety and autonomy.

GDC-RR-30c990ff8f.title: Understanding Primary Care Provider Decisions Regarding Referral to Early Intervention for Children with Developmental Delays.
GDC-RR-30c990ff8f.authors: Reinitz MO, Fitzgerald Z, Tangkilisan G, Sanders B, Junqua J, King-Hails L, Solgi M, Zuckerman KE.
GDC-RR-30c990ff8f.abstract:
Objective

While the gap between children identified with developmental conditions and those receiving services has been previously established, less is known regarding the role PCP decision-making plays in service delays.This study aims to explore PCP perspectives on factors influencing their decisions to refer/not refer children with positive developmental screens to Early Intervention (EI) services.

Methods

We conducted qualitative interviews with 15 PCPs from 7 Oregon clinics focusing on general counseling strategies and referral decision making after a positive developmental screen. PCPs were providers who participated in Autism ALERT, a pilot trial of family navigation for children with autism symptoms. Interviews had two parts. Part 1 assessed PCPs' general counseling strategies about Developmental Disabilities (DD) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) screening. Part 2 explored clinical reasoning and management decisions through chart stimulated recall. Each interview was audio recorded and transcribed. Interviews were coded by 2-3 team members using a phenomenological approach to deduce main themes.

Results

Three main interconnected themes and 10 subthemes emerged. Main themes included Screening Tool Results (e.g. severity of results and results reliability), Primary Care Provider's Clinical Judgement (e.g. trust with family and clinical judgement), and Familial Context (e.g. readiness for referral and level of concern). When these three themes were in conflict versus aligned, the decision to refer/not refer was subjected to providers' individual judgement.

Conclusion

Understanding the complexities of EI referral decision making may raise awareness of barriers to referral and improve early referral practices.

GDC-RR-00baf00c43.title: Recent trends of infant motor activity estimation using wearable sensors: A scoping review.
GDC-RR-00baf00c43.authors: DeVito A, Inamdar K, O'Neil ME, Zhu Y, Alam MAU, Koren A.
GDC-RR-00baf00c43.abstract: Wearable sensors may enable objective monitoring of infant motor activity, posture, and movement in laboratory, clinic, and home contexts. However, evidence for the validity, generalizability, and implementation readiness of wearable-derived infant motor measures remains heterogeneous. This scoping review synthesized technical features, validation evidence, and clinical applications of wearable sensors monitoring infant motor activity, posture, or movement during awake periods in the first year of life. PRISMA-ScR guidelines were followed, and the protocol was prospectively registered on Open Science Framework. Searches for peer-reviewed articles on wearable-based monitoring of infant activity published between 2019 and 2024 were identified through searches of PubMed, CINAHL, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library. A total of 41 studies were selected and classified using Keadle's five-phase validation framework, distinguishing technical validation (Phases I-III) from applied implementation (Phase IV). Fifteen studies (36.6%) included typically developing infants, 22 (53.7%) included infants with or at-risk for developmental disabilities, and 4 (9.8%) were unspecified. Fifteen studies (36.6%) focused on technical validation; 26 (63.4%) implemented sensors in applied contexts. Triaxial accelerometers (n = 15) and IMUs (n = 24) were most common, with sampling frequencies from 1-150 Hz. Posture classification accuracy was 95.8%-98.2% in studies directly comparing posture and movement, whereas fine-grained movement classification was near 81%-84%. Reference-standard correspondence was generally strong for accumulated posture duration (r = 0.80-0.99) but more variable for movement and clinical measures (r = 0.61-0.98). Application studies quantified physical activity, movement coordination and complexity, and intervention responsiveness, with over half collecting home-based data. Wearable sensors have evolved from proof-of-concept systems to family-centered digital health tools supporting developmental monitoring and physical activity promotion. When paired with caregiver feedback and infant-centered design, these technologies may support families, complement clinic-based assessment, and extend developmental support access. Future research should prioritize standardized reporting, affordability, and open-source analytic pipelines to advance equitable implementation.

GDC-RR-ce0516cd06.title: THE IMPACT OF GLOBAL YOUTH MOVEMENTS ON INDIAN YOUTH (2020–OCTOBER 2026) A Sociological Study of Political Consciousness, Digital Activism and Social Change
GDC-RR-ce0516cd06.abstract: A new wave of youth movements has emerged globally in the third decade of the twenty-first century. Between 2020 and October 2026, young people in various countries staged large-scale protests against corruption, unemployment, inflation, weaknesses in education systems, the crisis of political representation, social inequality, human-rights violations and restrictions on freedom of expression. A distinctive feature of these movements has been the important role played not only by traditional organisations but also by social media, digital networks, online campaigns and decentralised leadership. Youth activism in Myanmar, Thailand, the United States, Nigeria, Sri Lanka, Iran, Bangladesh, Kenya, Indonesia, Nepal, Serbia, Morocco, Madagascar, the Philippines and European countries such as France, Italy and Spain has influenced political and social debates. By October 2026, the movements emerging in Europe had foregrounded the quality of education, the housing crisis, the rising cost of living, employment insecurity and the condition of public services. This research article presents a sociological study of the possible effects of global youth movements on Indian youth by analysing their nature, causes, forms and consequences. It uses the theories of relative deprivation, resource mobilisation and new social movements, along with the concept of the network society. The study concludes that global youth movements can encourage political awareness, sensitivity towards civil rights, digital participation and aspirations for social change among young people. However, the success of a movement is not confined to protests; it also requires democratic institutions, policy reforms and sustained social participation

GDC-RR-bafc7bb71a.title: National support for a healthy checkout policy: a randomised message-framing experiment.
GDC-RR-bafc7bb71a.authors: Gil AM, Reimold AE, Lemmon B, Wolf EC, Dorfman L, Brown SD, Au LE, Falbe J.
GDC-RR-bafc7bb71a.abstract:
Objective

Healthy checkout policies set nutritional standards for store checkouts and have been implemented in three US jurisdictions. We compared four message frames, each describing a different rationale for the policy, on adults' support for a healthy checkout policy.

Design

Participants were randomised to one of four message frames: (1) expanding healthy choices; (2) reducing parental stress by removing unhealthy items from child eye level; (3) improving community and child health; or (4) addressing predatory marketing. We used Poisson regression with robust standard errors to examine policy support by message frame and explore variation in support by socio-demographic characteristics.

Setting

Online randomised experiment.

Participants

A convenience sample of US adults (analytic N 3978) recruited online via quota-matching to approximate national socio-demographic characteristics.

Results

Overall, most participants (65 %) supported a healthy checkout policy. Support was moderately higher (68 %) when the policy was framed as reducing parental stress than addressing predatory marketing (64 %) or expanding healthy choices (61 %; all p < 0·05). Policy support was also higher when framed as improving community and child health (67 %) than expanding healthy choices (61 %; p < 0·01). In adjusted models, overall policy support was higher among adults with Hispanic ethnicity (68 %); incomes >$35 000 (range 66-70 %); a prediabetes or type 2 diabetes diagnosis (67 %); at least some college education (67 %) and residence in the Northeast US (70 %; all p < 0·05).

Conclusions

Support for a healthy checkout policy was high, especially when framed around benefits to child health. Adults with certain socio-demographic and clinical characteristics may especially support healthy checkout policies.

GDC-RR-e0121857da.title: Religious Communities and Social Media in North Macedonia: Between Digital Presence and Online Engagement
GDC-RR-e0121857da.authors: Aleksandar Grizhev, Ivan Blazhevski, Ruzica Cacanoska
GDC-RR-e0121857da.abstract: Religious communities increasingly operate within digital environments where institutional communication, religious practice, and audience interaction intersect. Yet, establishing a presence on social media does not necessarily translate into meaningful engagement or dialogue. This study examines how the principal religious communities in North Macedonia use social media platforms and how their institutional communication practices are reflected in the digital public sphere. Drawing on an exploratory qualitative content analysis conducted between January and June 2025, this research examines institutional and institutionally associated Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube accounts of the principal religious communities in the country while considering selected smaller communities where relevant. The analysis focuses on platform presence, posting practices, types of content, language use, multimedia formats, institutional organization, and patterns of interaction with followers. The findings reveal substantial differences in the visibility, intensity, and sophistication of digital communication across religious communities. However, despite greater use of multimedia, multilingual communication, and more frequent posting among some actors, communication remains predominantly oriented toward dissemination rather than sustained dialogue. More interactive practices are observed mainly in youth-oriented and community-focused accounts. This study argues that digital presence, dissemination, engagement, and dialogue should be understood as distinct but overlapping dimensions of institutional religious communication. It also contributes to the study of digital religion by examining these dynamics in a religiously plural Southeast European context.

 Preface
The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) is the UK’s independent regulator for information rights
legislation. This includes the Data Protection Act 2018 and the UK General Data Protection Regulation
(UKGDPR). In September 2021, the ICO’s Age Appropriate Design Code (AADC or Children’s code), a
statutory code, came into force. This requires organisations which are offering online services likely to be
accessed by children to conform to 15 standards. Standard three of the code sets an expectation that online
platforms either establish the age of their users with an appropriate degree of certainty, or apply the standards
in the code to all users.
Ofcom has a statutory duty to promote and research media literacy, including in respect of material available on
the internet. A key way it seeks to fulfil this duty is through its Making Sense of Media programme, which aims
to help improve the online skills, knowledge and understanding of children and adults in the UK. Ofcom was
also given powers in autumn 2020 to regulate UK-established video-sharing platforms (VSPs). And in December
2020, the Government confirmed its intention to nominate Ofcom as the regulator for online safety in the UK,
under the Online Safety Bill.
The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF) brings together four UK regulators tasked with regulating
digital services to collectively drive greater regulatory co-operation and deliver coherent approaches to digital
regulation. Through the DRCF workplan for 2022-23, the ICO and Ofcom committed to working together on
protecting children online and synchronising their efforts – with a particular focus on improving outcomes for
children and parents – by ensuring privacy and online safety protections work in unison. This includes joint
research on age assurance, as well as a joint working framework to support the oversight of Ofcom’s Video
Sharing Platform (VSP) regulatory framework and the ICO’s Children’s code.
This research will also inform Ofcom’s preparations for implementing the new online safety laws, as referenced
in Ofcom’s Roadmap to Online Safety Regulation. As part of these preparations, Ofcom is building a robust
evidence base, bringing together internal and external data, collected using different methods, from a variety of
different sources. This programme of research will further develop Ofcom’s understanding of online harms and
how it can help to promote a safer user experience.
Age Assurance Research
Age assurance refers to a number of measures which would allow organisations to prevent children from
accessing services which are inappropriate for their age, and also to tailor services to suit their developmental
needs 1.
The role of age assurance in children’s use of online services is an area of mutual interest for both the ICO and
Ofcom as age assurance products that comply with data protection legislation and meet further online safety
objectives will help to deliver a stronger, more positive outcome for children online. Given it is an area where
there are interlinking responsibilities, this research has been commissioned to aid coherence between these two
bodies and will help to inform policies and guidance in this area.
This research provides an understanding of the attitudes parents and children have about age assurance. The
research shows there is parental and child support for the principle of age assurance, but also recognises some
methods raise concerns related to privacy, parental control, child autonomy and usability.
